name: Pulmonary hypertension due to lung disease/hypoxia (group 3)

reference.source: ESC/ERS Guidelines for Pulmonary Hypertension / Nunn's Applied Respiratory Physiology
clinicalPearls: Arises in chronic lung disease and hypoxaemic states, notably COPD, interstitial lung disease, combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema, and sleep-disordered breathing
Alveolar hypoxia is the central driver, causing hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and, over time, vascular remodelling and destruction of the capillary bed
The pulmonary hypertension is usually mild to moderate and proportionate to the severity of the lung disease, so severe pressures out of proportion should prompt a search for another cause
Presents as worsening breathlessness, hypoxaemia, and eventually right heart failure (cor pulmonale) superimposed on the underlying respiratory condition
Long-term oxygen therapy for chronic hypoxaemia is the cornerstone of management, alongside optimal treatment of the underlying lung disease
Group 1 targeted pulmonary vasodilators are generally not recommended, as they can worsen ventilation-perfusion matching and gas exchange
A severe pulmonary vascular phenotype with only modest airflow or parenchymal impairment warrants referral to a specialist centre
reference.pathophysiology: Pulmonary hypertension due to lung disease and hypoxia is driven principally by alveolar hypoxia, which provokes hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction as an adaptive mechanism to divert blood away from poorly ventilated lung. When hypoxia is chronic and widespread, this vasoconstriction becomes sustained and is accompanied by structural remodelling of the pulmonary arteries with medial hypertrophy and intimal thickening. In parenchymal diseases such as emphysema and fibrosis, destruction and distortion of the alveolar-capillary bed reduces the cross-sectional area of the pulmonary vasculature, further raising resistance. Acidosis and hypercapnia potentiate the vasoconstriction, and the chronically elevated afterload leads to right ventricular hypertrophy and eventual failure. The pulmonary hypertension is typically proportionate to the underlying disease, and a disproportionately severe pattern suggests an additional or alternative process.
additionalDifferentials: Pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease (group 2)
Idiopathic or heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension coexisting with lung disease
Connective tissue disease with combined lung and vascular involvement
additionalInvestigations: Pulmonary function tests including diffusing capacity to characterise the lung disease
High-resolution CT of the chest to define parenchymal and airway disease
Arterial blood gases and overnight oximetry or sleep study for hypoxaemia and hypoventilation
Transthoracic echocardiography to estimate pressures and assess right ventricular function
Right heart catheterisation when a severe or disproportionate pulmonary vascular phenotype is suspected
Ventilation-perfusion scan to exclude chronic thromboembolic disease
redFlags: Pulmonary hypertension severe out of proportion to the degree of lung disease
Rapidly progressive right heart failure or worsening hypoxaemia
Deterioration in gas exchange after inappropriate use of pulmonary vasodilators
reference.prognosis: The presence of pulmonary hypertension marks more advanced lung disease and predicts reduced exercise capacity and survival, with a severe pulmonary vascular phenotype carrying the worst outlook. Correcting chronic hypoxaemia with oxygen and optimising the underlying respiratory disease can slow progression, but the pulmonary hypertension is rarely fully reversible.
pitfalls: Treating mild proportionate pulmonary hypertension with group 1 targeted therapy and worsening gas exchange
Failing to investigate a disproportionately severe pattern for thromboembolic or arterial disease
Overlooking correctable nocturnal hypoxaemia or sleep-disordered breathing
Attributing all breathlessness to the airways or parenchyma and missing evolving cor pulmonale
Not referring a severe pulmonary vascular phenotype to a specialist pulmonary hypertension centre
references: ESC/ERS Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Pulmonary Hypertension
